articles.title: Govee would like to make your smart holiday lights Matter
articles.summary: Govee’s newest holiday string lights and strip lights come with Matter support and improved colors.
articles.body: At IFA 2024, Govee revealed launch dates for a veritable rat king of Matter-enabled decorative lighting. These include smart string lights, curtain lights, and Govee’s first icicle-style smart lights. The company also has two sets of strip lights to follow up its M1 Matter strip, and... listen, it’s a lot of lights. ‘Tis (sort of, almost) the season, so let’s start with Govee’s new holiday lights. The company says all are IP65 waterproof-rated, so they should be good for indoor or outdoor installation, and they’re all Matter-compatible, meaning you can use them with any smart home ecosystem that uses the one smart home standard to rule them all. All are coming to the US and the EU. [Image: Govee says its new curtain lights have improved custom effects. Coming first are the Govee Curtain Lights 2 on September 20th. Govee says these will be brighter than the previous version and that custom effects such as user-provided animated GIFs or those picked from Govee’s library have been improved. They also sport Govee’s “AI Lighting Bot,” which lets you create effects by describing them either in text or with your voice. You will be able to pick them up in packs of one ($149.99), two ($259.99), or three ($399.99). Govee is also releasing a follow-up to our last year’s pick for cheap smart holiday string lights. The company says its Christmas String Lights 2 use RGBW beads and come with a new “Smart Mapping” feature for setting up effects. They will start at $99.99 for a 20-meter string going up to $399.99 for 100 meters and will be released September 25th. Govee is also releasing new icicle-style lights in 10-meter ($139.99) and 20-meter ($249.99) versions. These are a new style for the company and will be available on September 29th. Govee Strip Lights [Image: Govee’s new Strip Light 2 Pro gets a new chip to drive its colors. Govee is also releasing two new strip lights, following the company’s M1 LED strip light that The Verge’s Jennifer Pattison Tuohy found to be bright, colorful, and broadly compatible, thanks to its Matter support. The new Strip Light 2 Pro and COB Strip Light Pro also work with the new smart home standard. The Strip Light 2 Pro uses RGBWW LEDs and gets a new chip that offers more color depth. It costs $59.99 for two-meter strips, $99.99 for five meters, and $149.99 for 10 meters. The COB Strip Light Pro uses a chip-on-board LED design encased in silicon to diffuse the light, which ought to make light transitions along the strip smoother — more gradient, less obviously individual diodes. The COB Strip Light Pro will be $99.99 for three meters and $149.99 for a five-meter version. Both strip lights are out on September 10th. Govee’s other intros [Image: The Star Light Projector (Aurora) makes your walls quite spacey. Okay, so it’s not all string-shaped. Govee also announced its Star Light Projector (Aurora) and AI Sync Box 2. The $79.99 Aurora beams 16-million-color “customizable aurora effects” onto surfaces up to 650 square inches and features a built-in Bluetooth speaker that’s also got 18 white noise sounds. And finally, on October 14th, Govee will release the AI Sync Box Kit 2. This one is the latest ambient TV backlighting gadget that the company has been playing around with for a few years. (See our Govee Immersion review from 2021.) Announced at CES this year, the new Sync Box uses HDMI 2.1 passthrough to produce AI-generated effects for things like video games. It can pass up to 8K resolution at 60Hz or 4K at 120Hz — a step up from the 4K-limited HDMI 2.0 of the previous AI Sync Box Kit.

articles.title: Insta360 redesigned its compact action cam with a bigger battery and swappable storage
articles.summary: The Insta360 Go Ultra has a new square-shaped design with a larger battery and a microSD card slot.
articles.body: Insta360 has announced the next version of its compact Go action camera, which helped the company differentiate itself from established competitors like GoPro several years ago. As Insta360 teased earlier this week, the new Go Ultra not only breaks from the numbered naming convention of previous iterations, but it also ditches the camera’s distinctive pill shape for a rounded square design with an offset lens. It’s not the steepest price increase for the Go series – the Go 2 launched at $299 while the Go 3, which introduced a charging remote with a screen, was $380 – but the new Insta360 Go Ultra is $50 more expensive than last year’s Go 3S at $449.99. It’s available now in midnight black or arctic white through the company’s online store and Amazon, or as part of a $499.99 Creator Bundle that includes accessories like a mini tripod and a quick release mount. [Image: The Go Ultra cameras now feature an ambient light sensor and a compartment for a microSD card. The Insta360 Go Ultra measures 1.8 inches on each side, while the pill-shaped Go 3S was slightly longer but a bit narrower. The new model is also almost 14 grams heavier than the Go 3S (not counting its screen-equipped Action Pod accessory that adds another 109 grams), but the Go Ultra is still a much smaller action camera than alternatives like the DJI Osmo Action 5 Pro and even Insta360’s own Ace Pro 2. It features a new 1/1.28-inch sensor that’s considerably larger than what the Go 3S uses (and the same size as the sensor in Insta360’s X5 360-degree action cam), which, alongside a new ambient light sensor, should help improve the look of footage captured in low-light situations. The Go Ultra’s video capabilities still max out at 4K, but at 60fps, which is double the maximum frame rate of the Go 3S. Reducing the frame rate to 4K/30fps enables an “Active HDR” mode, while dropping the resolution to 1080p boosts frame rates to 240fps for capturing slo-mo footage. [Image: A new accessory lets you easily attach the Go Ultra camera to the brim of a hat. Even with the lens located in the corner, the Go Ultra’s square design could make it a little more challenging to determine when the camera is capturing footage in landscape versus portrait orientations. The previous pill shape made that a lot easier. But the new design has room for a much larger 500mAh battery that Insta360 says is good for up to 70 minutes of recording or up to 200 minutes when paired with the Action Pod, but at 1080p/24fps and the screen off. At 4K/60fps recording times on a full charge will potentially be shorter than that. [Image: There are several accessories for wearing or attaching the Go Ultra to standard action camera mounts, selfie sticks, or tripods. Instead of built-in storage, the Go Ultra now features a memory card slot supporting microSD cards up to 2TB in size, so you can swap in replacements as they fill up. It’s also still waterproof to depths of up to 33 feet. Accessories include an upgraded magnetic pendant for wearing the camera at chest level and a hat clip designed for toddlers, but the back of the Go Ultra is also magnetic, which means it can be mounted directly to many metallic surfaces. articles.title: Oh snap, I have a new favorite phone grip
articles.summary: In the war of double-sided magnetic phone grips, Syncwire and OhSnap Snap Grip 5 are the best I’ve tried.
articles.body: In 2022, we called a simple magnetic ring from Anker the best MagSafe phone grip, but things have evolved dramatically since then! You can buy two or even three magnetic rings joined at the hip these days to wield your iPhone, recent Pixel, or really any phone if you stick a magnetic case or included mounting ring on the back. But the best I’ve yet tried are the double-sided $15-$25 Syncwire Magnetic Phone Ring Holder — and, more recently, the $40 OhSnap Snap Grip 5. [Media: Unlike the Anker we swore by for years, both are double-sided magnet rings. I don’t have to take them off when I plop them on a MagSafe phone charger or car mount. And with them on, I can stick my phone directly to a fridge, filing cabinet, or certain pieces of gym equipment since the magnets work both ways. But the real trick, the thing that sets them apart from the pack, is getting the right magnet strength. The OhSnap 5 now uses magnets so strong that it no longer needs any pesky adhesive to hold onto my phone — while the reverse side is just strong enough to stick to my magnetic car mount while also detaching easily. My wife’s puffier version of the Syncwire also detaches easily, as I discussed in my September video below, but the standard version doesn’t. I often have to run back out to the car after accidentally leaving my Syncwire stuck to the charger. [Media: As you’ll see in my videos embedded in this story, the Syncwire’s a pretty traditional ring save for its awesome ratcheting mechanism, which leaves fewer scrapes on my phone than the Anker and doubles as an excellent fidget toy. The OhSnap works differently: instead of putting a finger through a ring, you place them in or around a set of interlocking flexible arms attached to a disc that retracts from the back. It looks downright weird but it’s impressively versatile: you can hold it between any two fingers like a PopSocket, or stick any of your fingers into the little cage between the arms. You can even slot the disc into a little notch to turn it into a basic phone stand. You can see all those in my October 2024 video about the earlier Snap Grip 4 version: [Media: $40 is a high price to pay for a phone grip, particularly one that’s had some sort of weakness in every revision so far. (My colleague Victoria Song broke her Snap Grip 3’s little fingers, the Snap Grip 4 had far stronger fingers but it also had the annoying adhesive, and now the new soft-touch coating is peeling off my Snap Grip 5 after a month or so of use, though it’s easy enough to scrape away.) But the Snap Grip 5 is meaningfully thinner and lighter than the Syncwire, and I no longer accidentally leave it in the car. As a cheapskate and fidget toy lover, I might stick with my ratcheting Syncwire… but I’m definitely thinking I might gift a Snap Grip or two this Christmas! Oh, and before you ask, my phone case is the Spigen Ultra Hybrid ZeroOne Edition. A lot of people ask!

articles.title: Govee’s latest smart lights can make your ceiling more interesting
articles.summary: Govee announced the Sky Ceiling Light and Ceiling Light Ultra at CES 2026. No prices or launch dates have been shared.
articles.body: Govee is known for putting lights in every corner of your room: in your bulb sockets, in the corner for a little multicolored bias lighting, and even behind the TV with its scene-matching LED strips. And it has some curious announcements at CES 2026 that tackle a new part of the room: the ceiling. Govee has announced the Sky Ceiling Light and the Ceiling Light Ultra. The Sky Ceiling Light, shown above, is designed to mimic daylight, so as to present the illusion that you have a view to the great outdoors. Govee envisions this being a worthwhile addition for windowless spaces, saying that it has “refined white-light performance” that can create a “calming, uplifting atmosphere” wherever you choose to install it. The company says it uses custom LEDs to boost the realism of its color transitions from daylight to sunset. Its lights can go from 2,700K to 6,500K, with a max brightness of 5,200 lumens at 6,500K color temperature. Pricing and availability haven’t been announced. [Image: The Ceiling Light Ultra is being billed as “the industry’s first ceiling light designed as a true creative canvas.” Govee is touting that this model features 616 RGB LEDs that can be controlled individually, which it claims is among the highest LED densities in the category. It’s a light that can display over 20 lighting effect presets as well as your own creations. It kind of looks like a supersized and more capable version of the little screen on the original HomePod. The Govee app features AI Lighting Bot 2.0, which converts your text prompts into lighting arrangements that can be displayed on this model. No pricing or availability info for this one, either.

articles.title: Roborock launches its first robot lawn mower in the US
articles.summary: Roborock’s next robot lawn mower, the RockMow X1 LiDAR, is coming to the US. Unveiled at CES 2026, the bot will arrive later this year with 360-degree 3D scanning.
articles.body: Roborock is finally bringing its bots to yards in the US, several months after expanding into robot lawn mowers last year. The Roborock RockMow X1 LiDAR, announced today at CES, will be launching later this year, featuring autonomous navigation, all-wheel drive, and 360-degree 3D scanning using a combination of LiDAR and Visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (VSLAM). Like the earlier RockMow Z1, the RockMow X1 LiDAR can handle slopes of up to 80 percent and traverse obstacles up to 3.1 inches high. According to Roborock, it can mow up to half an acre (about 2,000 square meters) per day, notably less than the 5,000 square meters the Z1 is capable of. The RockMow X1 LiDAR will face some competition in the US, including from other lawn-mowing bots that also use LiDAR.

articles.title: Dreame brings 8K video to compact action cameras
articles.summary: The Leaptic Cube is Dreame’s first action camera with features that could give DJI and Insta360 more competition.
articles.body: Dreame, a Chinese company known for its unique robot vacuums and floor cleaners, expanded its offerings at CES 2026, such as a $700 floor lamp that doubled as a hair dryer. But more interesting is the debut of the company’s first action camera. The Leaptic Cube features a design similar to the DJI Osmo Nano and Insta360 Go Ultra, allowing you to separate the compact camera from its screen so you can mount it in different places while still being able to see what you’re capturing. But while those cameras max out at a 4K resolution, Dreame’s does 8K. The Leaptic Cube features a 1/1.3-inch sensor, the same size DJI uses in the Osmo Nano, paired with a 155-degree wide-angle lens so it can capture more light to improve video quality, even when recording after the sun sets. Capturing at 8K limits the Cube’s framerate to 30fps, but the extra pixels provide more room to crop and reframe footage afterwards and facilitates the camera’s built-in stabilization. Dropping the resolution to 4K boosts the frame rate to 60fps with HDR, or up to 120fps for capturing slo-mo footage. [Image: The Cube’s camera can be separated from the screen and used up to 98 feet away while still streaming a live preview of what you’re capturing. Dreame says the Cube’s battery life can be extended to up to 220 minutes when using a “magnetically attached external battery dock,” and that the camera can be attached to its 2.27-inch screen facing forwards or back, so you can use it to frame selfies. Other features include a proprietary wireless transmission system with a range of around 98 feet, AI-powered tracking and auto-framing, and an AI assistant that can be used to control the camera with voice commands while it’s connected to a mobile app. What we don’t yet know is pricing, or when Dreame plans to launch the Leaptic Cube.

articles.title: MacBook Neo review: the Mac for the masses
articles.summary: Apple’s MacBook Neo is its cheapest Mac laptop yet, starting at $599. It’s also the first MacBook to come with an A18 Pro chip from an iPhone.
articles.body: The MacBook Neo is basically the M1 MacBook Air all over again. That laptop changed the game in 2020, and became the default option for just about anyone who wanted a great all-around thin-and-light laptop and could spend $1,000. The M1 Air was good enough that you could still buy a new one until last month. The Neo takes its place as Apple’s cheapest laptop, with a starting price of $599 and enough power to handle everyday tasks and last all day on a charge. It’s designed to entice students and first-time laptop buyers into Apple’s world. It will. The Air is still better than the Neo in pretty much every way, but even the cheapest MacBook Neo is good enough to be the go-to Apple laptop for a lot of people. Actually, not just the go-to Apple laptop; the Neo’s hardware simultaneously embarrasses an entire class of affordable (and even far pricier) Windows laptops, as well as just about any Chromebook. And the thing runs on an iPhone chip. [Product: Apple MacBook Neo | The Neo is “it just works” at a lower price. The 13-inch screen is vivid, bright, and pleasant to look at. It even gets bright enough to comfortably use outside in all but direct glare. The speakers sound full for their size, and cranking the volume can fill a small room with music. They don’t get as loud or bassy as the four- and six-speaker setups in pricier MacBooks, and by comparison they sound thinner, but for dual side-firing speakers they’re A-OK. And the Neo’s speakers are much better than the average ones found in cheap or even midrange Windows laptops. Just be mindful that you’re likely to muffle them when grabbing the sides of the Neo. --- Component report card * Screen: B * Webcam: B * Keyboard: C * Trackpad: A * Port selection: D for #donglelife * Speakers: B * Number of ugly stickers to remove: 0 --- Typing on the Neo feels like other current MacBooks. The key travel isn’t as deep as on some Lenovo and Asus keyboards that I prefer, but it’s not too shallow, like the butterfly switch-era MacBooks were. It’s a bummer there’s no backlight illumination, but at least three of the four color combos have bright, near-white keycaps (which helps just a tiny bit). Another just-fine component of the Neo is its 1080p webcam, which looks sharp and clear, even in low light, but lacks the higher resolution and Center Stage auto-framing of the current MacBook Airs and Pros. The Neo’s most interesting hardware compromise is its mechanical trackpad. It’s missing Apple’s Force Touch, but who cares? I never use it. You know what’s more important? A mechanical trackpad that clicks anywhere — corner to corner, just like Apple’s haptic trackpads. It even feels similar to the haptic ones, but with a slightly chunkier click sound and smaller surface area. The Neo’s trackpad sets the bar for mechanical trackpads, easily outclassing all the just-okay trackpads out there that have stiff, piano-key-style top hinges where the top third doesn’t even click. I’ve tested much more expensive Windows laptops that make major compromises on their screen, speaker, keyboard, trackpad or webcam quality — or more than one, so the fact that the Neo has no major flaws is a big deal. I wouldn’t mind if the device were a little bit lighter, though; the Neo is the same solid-feeling 2.7 pounds as the 13-inch MacBook Air. Asus has a 16-inch laptop coming out that weighs less than the Neo. Regardless, Apple is putting on a clinic with this complete package at $599, especially when you also consider its performance. [Table: MacBook Neo benchmarks] --- I answered some of your questions about the MacBook Neo. I hosted an AMA on the MacBook Neo for Verge subscribers, and you can check out all the questions and my answers here. --- The MacBook Neo zips through the light workloads it’s designed for. The A18 Pro chip actually outperforms Apple’s M1 MacBook Air (and most Windows laptops) in single-core processing benchmarks, the spec most vital for the everyday productivity stuff the Neo is meant to handle. That’s why this $600 laptop excels at light tasks like web browsing and working on Google Docs. The Neo’s 8GB of RAM and slow 256GB storage are totally adequate for living this life, but the machine does feel a little slower at the fringes if you know where to look — like how clicking the Applications folder on the dock sometimes takes a second for the icons to populate. The relatively paltry RAM and storage prevent the Neo from performing as well in heavier creative apps as the MacBook Airs and Pros, but that’s fine. Think of the Neo as more Canva and CapCut than Photoshop and Premiere. I pushed the Neo to its limits by opening over 60 Chrome tabs across four desktops, one of which was playing a 1080p YouTube video of The Vergecast, and I kept Slack, Signal, Steam, Messages, and Apple Music all running simultaneously. The Neo slowed to a crawl amid that chaos, especially while swiping between those desktops. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The Neo also struggled with my usual Lightroom Classic editing. I could browse through image previews of around 300 50-megapixel RAW files just fine, but diving into the Develop module for actual processing meant sitting through many turns of the spinning beach ball of death. I managed a full edit of around 55 final images with some batch processing, but it was painful to slog through. It’s also, I repeat, not what the Neo is for. Apple tempts you to upgrade from the base Neo, and if you can, you should, even though it won’t solve all your problems. The $599 model has 8GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. But for $699 the storage is doubled and you get a Touch ID sensor in the power button. The upgrade is completely worth it (especially if the $100 student discount makes it effectively free). A fingerprint sensor is much more convenient than typing in your password every time you wake your laptop. And with rising prices from the memory chip shortage, it’s no longer trivial to supplement your laptop’s limited storage with a quality external SSD. We weren’t able to test the 512GB version of the Neo, but it’s possible that like other MacBooks it could have faster read / write speeds than the base 256GB — which would help. It’s a little disheartening not to have even the option for 16GB of RAM two years after Apple finally made it standard on every other MacBook. But for students making basic class presentations, or folks doing office work, 8GB should be fine. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: When I used it for things like web browsing across 20-ish Chrome tabs, Slack / Signal messaging, watching an occasional video or Twitch stream, and listening to music, everything hummed along smoothly. And it managed to last more than a full workday on battery. I got just under nine hours of battery life with the screen mostly kept on at 75 percent brightness. (I had my lockscreen set to a 20-minute time-out.) That workday also encompassed a Google Meet call lasting nearly 40 minutes and nearly two hours of Apple Music streaming at low-to-medium volume. Windows laptops that also do this often have much bigger batteries and cost more than $599. Apple only includes a 20W USB-C charger, though when I plugged the Neo into a 140W charger, it did charge at up to 30W. That’s not particularly impressive considering the iPhone 17 can charge at 40W. Unlike the Airs and Pros, the MacBook Neo doesn’t have a MagSafe connector, just two USB-C ports — one 10Gbps USB 3 and one USB 2.0, both on the left-hand side, of course. They’re unmarked, which is just silly, but the USB 3 is at the back, closer to the hinge, and if you plug an external monitor into the front port, you’ll get a notification alerting you. Either can be used for charging. Even at 30W, it took around 45 to 50 minutes to charge from zero to 50 percent, and another hour to get it all the way to 100 percent. That’s not outlandish, but you’re not getting any quick top-ups. And the charging cable Apple includes in the box is annoyingly short at five feet / 1.5m (half a meter shorter than the MagSafe cable included with other MacBooks). [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: There will always be cheaper laptops than the MacBook Neo, but you’d be hard-pressed to find something cheaper and better, or even the same price and better, without a bunch of compromises somewhere. If you need or want more RAM, a better screen, a faster processor, and more, faster ports, the Neo is not for you — that’s what the Air and Pro are for. But the Neo is the new default recommendation for students and laptop newcomers who want something easy to use with minimal fuss. I wouldn’t expect a Neo to last quite as long as an Air with more RAM, but the more affordable price makes it a more than worthwhile on-ramp — especially because most people don’t want or need to spend $1,000 on a laptop. Apple now has the perfect laptop for that crowd. And a few years down the line when they decide it’s not quite powerful enough, Apple has the perfect laptop for that, too. Photography by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge --- 2026 Apple MacBook Neo specs (as reviewed) * Display: 13-inch (2408 x 1506) 60Hz IPS LED * CPU: Apple A18 Pro * RAM: 8GB unified memory * Storage: 256GB SSD * Webcam: 1080p FaceTime HD camera * Connectivity: Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 6 * Ports: 1x USB 3 (Type C) up to 10Gbps with DisplayPort, 1x USB 2.0 (Type C) up to 480Mbps, 3.5mm combo audio jack * Biometrics: None (Touch ID fingerprint sensor optional on 512GB configuration) * Weight: 2.7 pounds / 1.23kg * Dimensions: 11.71 x 8.12 x 0.5 inches / 297.5 x 206.4 x 12.7mm * Battery: 36.5Whr * Price: $599 --- Update, March 11th: Updated scorecard text to clarify the Neo’s default charging speeds

articles.title: The new PopSockets grip is so thin you’ll forget it’s even there
articles.summary: PopSockets new Low-Pro is an ultra-slim magnetic phone grip just 2.6mm thick that also includes a fold-out stand.
articles.body: If you had asked me a week ago to recommend a thinner alternative to PopSockets’ magnetic phone grips, I would have told you to buy the OhSnap Snap Grip 5. Ask me now and I’ll redirect you right back to the company that accidentally invented the phone grip in 2012 when trying to come up with a better way to wrangle Apple EarPods. PopSockets’ new Low-Pro is its slimmest phone grip yet, and it’s not only thinner than OhSnap’s latest, it’s also more functional and more comfortable to hold. Available starting today exclusively through Apple in four colors (it will be available from PopSockets’ online store and other retailers starting on July 29th), the $39.99 Low-Pro Grip is launching at the same price as the Snap Grip 5. I’ve been a devoted fan of OhSnap’s grips for the past few years and recently upgraded to the Grip 5, but after testing the PopSockets Low-Pro for just a week, I’m ready to jump ship. [Product: PopSockets Low-Pro Grip | The last PopSockets grip I used was the Kick-Out Grip and Stand that debuted last year and did a better job than the OhSnap Grip 4 as a phone stand that worked well in both portrait and landscape mode. But at 7mm thick when collapsed, I found the Kick-Out Grip would occasionally get snagged when slipping my phone into my pocket. I’ve never had that problem with either the 2.5mm-thick Snap Grip 4 or the 3mm-thick Grip 5. The new PopSockets Low-Pro falls somewhere between OhSnap’s last two offerings at 2.6mm, which the company compares to the thickness of a pair of dimes or a toothpick. It’s definitely thin, but you have to look incredibly close to see the height difference when comparing the Low-Pro and Snap Grip 5 side by side. If you were going by touch alone the difference in thickness is imperceivable. [Image: [Image: Far more noticeable is how the two grips feel between your fingers when you’re holding your phone. The Snap Grip 5 carries forward a design that uses a set of interlocking flexible arms that attach the base of the grip to an extending disc. It’s a unique approach that OhSnap has improved and strengthened since The Verge’s Victoria Song had a Snap 3 Pro break nearly three years ago. But while the durability is better, the Snap Grip 5’s flexible arms still aren’t the most comfortable. They’re not painful by any means, but using the Snap Grip 5 has always felt to me like I’m sacrificing the comfort of a PopSockets grip for something more svelte. [Image: The Low-Pro’s pop-out disc connects to the grip’s base using a flexible material that folds flat when the grip is collapsed. With the Low-Pro, you get the best of both worlds. Instead of plastic arms or the traditional PopSockets design that features a collapsing squishy cone, the Low-Pro uses what the company describes as a “one-piece polymer” expansion layer connecting a pop-out disc to the grip’s base. It looks like a tube that’s been sliced full of diamond-shaped holes to help it collapse compactly, but it’s made out of a squishy material that makes the Low-Pro feel softer and more comfortable to hold at any angle. My fingers occasionally get sore during prolonged one-handed doomscrolling sessions using the Snap Grip 5, but that hasn’t been an issue with the Low-Pro. [Image: [Image: Both grips double as a phone stand, but the Low-Pro does it better. With the Snap Grip 5 you can tuck one edge of its extending disc into a notch on the base and use it to prop your phone up. But it’s limited to just one angle, and it works better with your phone laying sideways than standing up vertically. Surrounding the base of the Low-Pro is a hinged metal ring that folds out at any angle, so it works as a stand in either orientation. The base of the Low-Pro is a little wider than the Snap Grip 5 as a result, but the size difference is negligible. [Image: When removing several iPhones from magnetic wireless chargers, the Low-Pro grip would remain stuck to the charger instead of the phone. There is a reason to still consider OhSnap’s Snap Grip 5 over PopSockets’ Low-Pro. Both accessories allow your phone to stick to metal surfaces, magnetic mounts, and wireless chargers with the grips attached, but the magnets on the Snap Grip 5 are stronger than those in the Low-Pro. The Snap Grip 5 always remained securely attached to the back of my iPhone 16 Pro when removing it from a magnetic wireless charging stand, but the Low-Pro consistently remained behind stuck to the stand. [Image: The Low-Pro is more comfortable to hold than the Snap Grip 5, and its design lets you hold the grip at any angle. If you regularly mount your phone to magnetic accessories like this, such as relying on a car mount to use your phone as a GPS device, there’s a very good chance the Low-Pro could get frequently left behind and forgotten. If you don’t, then PopSockets’ new Low-Pro Grip is a worthy alternative. It’s not the thinnest grip ever created, but PopSockets has improved on OhSnap’s design in a few important areas that make a grip a tempting accessory, even if you’re trying to keep your phone as thin as possible. Photography by Andrew Liszewski / The Verge

articles.title: Satechi’s new MacBook Neo accessories color-match Apple’s budget-friendly laptop.

articles.title: Anker’s Soundcore is bringing its incredible call quality to more headphones
articles.summary: All the new headphones and earbuds use Anker’s Thus chip.
articles.body: After introducing the Thus processing chip in April and releasing it with the Liberty 5 Pro series earbuds, Soundcore is bringing it to more audio products. The Thus chip is behind the best call quality I’ve ever heard from a pair of earbuds or headphones, virtually eliminating ambient sounds from the speaker’s environment. At IFA 2026 in Berlin, Soundcore announced the Space 2 Pro headphones, AeroClip 2 and AeroClip 2 Pro open clip earbuds, and Liberty Buds 2. The Space 2 Pro will be the first headphones to use the Thus chip and use a 6-microphone array for voice isolation. There are also eight microphones for the headphones’ adaptive active noise cancellation (ANC), which Soundcore claims is 1.5 times stronger than the ANC on the Space One Pro headphones across the 20Hz to 2,000Hz frequency range. (This covers the most important sound distractions including airplane drones and HVAC systems, as well as normal conversation.) Soundcore’s latest version of its HearID listening preference test will create customized sound profiles, and the headphones support high-res audio via LDAC. Soundcore says the Space 2 Pro will get 60 hours of listening time at 50 percent volume (30 with ANC on) or 20 hours of talk time on a single charge. They launch on September 22 for $200, come in three colors — gray, white, and black — and will be available in the US, EU, and UK. Soundcore is also expanding its clip earbuds offerings, updating the AeroClip and adding a Pro version. The AeroClip 2 looks to be similar to the AeroClip, but with the Thus chip, will retail for $170 (the same price as the original AeroClip), and come in black, red, white, and blue at launch on September 22. The AeroClip 2 Pro will include Soundcore’s AI note-taking capability, which was also on the Liberty 5 Pro Max. But unlike the Liberty 5 Pro Max, with the AeroClip 2 Pro you can record online meetings and phone calls in addition to in-person interactions. The AeroClip 2 Pro includes a free AI transcription starter plan with 120 minutes per month for 24 months and the ability to subscribe for more transcription minutes. The 2 Pro clip earbuds use 11mm dual-diaphragm drivers, support LDAC hi-res audio, and should provide 10 hours of playback at 50 percent volume, with 30 hours total with the charging case. There’s no firm launch date or pricing yet for the 2 Pro, but we expect them later this year. Finally, the Soundcore Liberty Buds 2 are small, 4.7-gram earbuds. They will also include the Thus chip for call clarity and use a 6-microphone ANC system. The Liberty Buds 2 will be available in purple, black, and white on September 22 for $130.

articles.title: Now you can tell the Hue app how you want your smart lights to work
articles.summary: Philips Hue’s automation engine gets an AI makeover, and its buttons and switches will control your Sonos speakers.
articles.body: Philips Hue’s AI assistant can now build automations based on natural language, letting you describe what you want your lights to do. The feature, called Custom AI Behaviors, goes beyond simply changing colors or creating a scene and lets users orchestrate complex automations that weren’t previously achievable in the Hue app. Announced at a press event at the IFA tech show this week, Custom AI Behaviors joins a new integration with Sonos speakers. Users can control Sonos speakers with select Hue switches, including the Hue Tap Dial Switch, to trigger Favorites, play or pause audio, adjust the volume, and move to the next or previous song in a playlist. It will be available via a software update in November. [Image: Custom AI Behaviors allow you to use natural language to control all the capabilities of devices connected to your Hue lighting system. Many advanced Hue users probably already have sophisticated automations to control their lights, but they didn’t set them up in the Hue app, which is fairly limited beyond basic automations based around time of day. Hue’s head of technology, George Yianni, said this was mostly due to the UI complexity required to present these more advanced automations, not limitations in the technology. With Custom AI Behaviors, you’ll be able to tell the Hue AI Assistant in the app what you want. For example, when I’m asleep, turn on any lights triggered at nightlight setting; when I’m awake, use normal time-based color temperature. The system requires an input to know whether you’re awake or asleep (such as pressing a button to trigger a sleep or wake routine), but it can figure out the rest from there. [Image: Custom AI Behaviors requires the processing power of the Bridge Pro, and won’t work on other Hue bridges. You can also use Custom AI Behaviors to program Hue’s switches, which can be a fiddly process. One scenario demoed included asking the system to program button 4 on the Hue dimmer switch to disable the dining room motion sensor. This sounds like a great way to stop your lights turning on every 5 minutes while you’re watching TV because your dog is pacing, speaking from experience. Custom AI Behaviors are currently in beta and will roll out next month. The automation engine that runs them will be available to third-party developers. Yianni said the capabilities are vast, as every resource the bridge knows about is available as both input and output, including light color, every button press, every sensor event, and time. “It would have been hard to build a UI for this, but now LLMs provide a solution to the problem — they are able to expose richness of capability in an easy way,” he said. “This is not AI for the sake of AI; it’s a practical application of the technology.” [Image: To create a Custom AI Behavior, you type what you want into the app. It then offers you the option to accept or adjust the output. You can go back to a behavior to change or add to it. Custom AI Behaviors are exclusive to Hue’s latest bridge, the Bridge Pro, where the engine and automation run locally, while the AI assistant runs in the cloud. “We designed a domain-specific language, a simplified programming language specifically to interact with the AI assistant in the cloud,” Yianni says. The feature was built on the open-weight GLM family of models. “Closed-source models sometimes just change in the background, and can quite significantly change the behavior of your use case,” says Yianni. “With the open-source ones you control what actually runs.” Finally, the company teased a much-wanted feature launching early next year: Back-up & Restore will allow users to back up their bridge settings to the Hue cloud. Photography by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

articles.title: Anker’s new printer works directly on fabrics
articles.summary: Anker’s personal fabric printer is expected to launch early next year as an easy way to personalize garments.
articles.body: After introducing a consumer-friendly UV printer last year capable of printing designs directly on materials like wood, metal, glass, and acrylic, Anker’s eufyMake brand is introducing a new machine that can print directly on fabrics. With an expected launch sometime in the spring of 2027, Anker hasn’t yet revealed an official name for the new machine, but its “personal fabric printer” will offer multiple ways to put photos or custom designs onto T-shirts, jeans, bags, and hats. The machine will be capable of both direct-to-garment printing where images are applied directly to soft, breathable fabrics, and direct-to-film printing where designs are first created on a film and then transferred to a wider variety of fabrics using a heat press. [Image: Anker’s new printer is designed to replace multiple machines used to apply unique designs or images to garments. Anker’s personal fabric printer can apply both techniques on a single garment (although not at the same time) and can accurately reproduce colors on both light and dark fabrics. The company hasn’t revealed many details about the printer’s features and is not yet ready to talk pricing, but Anker claims the machine’s direct-to-garment capabilities will also work on embroidered designs. So instead of having to invest in an expensive multicolor embroidery machine to create colorful stitched designs, Anker’s machine can be paired with a cheaper single-color embroiderer and used to apply colors to the stitches afterwards.

articles.title: Philips Hue adds Nanoleaf’s light panels to its ecosystem with a $40 module
articles.summary: The smart lighting rivals team up to bring a deep integration between their products.
articles.body: Philips Hue is finally adding wall panels into its smart lighting portfolio. But instead of developing its own, it’s partnered with longtime rival Nanoleaf, the company that invented the smart modular wall panel category. Starting today, September 3rd, if you own Nanoleaf Hexagon, Triangle, or Mini Triangle wall panels, you can integrate them into your Philips Hue ecosystem using a Philips Hue x Nanoleaf Wall Light Module. The $39.99 device has a full Hue connectivity stack inside, running Bluetooth, Zigbee, and Thread concurrently — meaning you can use the Hue app and a Matter app like Apple Home simultaneously. Once in the Hue app, the module turns the panels into a full Hue light, capable of gradient light and compatible with Hue scenes, automations, switches, and entertainment experiences. They will also integrate with the new MotionAware and Spatial Aware features on the Bridge Pro. [Image: The Hue module is small and lightweight with no physical buttons. The module snaps onto the panels the same way Nanoleaf’s controller does, but today you have to use one or the other. George Yianni, founder and head of technology at Philips Hue, tells The Verge that the option to use both modules will be coming in the next couple of months. Until then, if you attach the Hue module, you’ll lose access to Nanoleaf’s dynamic scenes, screen mirroring, and music-reactive features. You also won’t have any physical controls for the light, something the Nanoleaf controller does offer. When dual control arrives, you can use both apps and the most recent software command will take priority, allowing you to switch between the functions of each ecosystem. [Image: [Image: However, you can only control the Nanoleaf panels in the Hue app, not the other way around. “This is more for people wanting Nanoleaf in their Hue ecosystem than using Hue in Nanoleaf,” Nanoleaf CEO Gimmy Chu told The Verge. Chu said he and Yianni have known each other for years and “dreamed about working together” (despite Hue’s parent company, Signify, recently suing Nanoleaf over patent infringement). Yianni said there is clear overlap in their customer base: “We often see our products installed together,” adding that wall panels have “been in our roadmap forever,” but were constantly pushed back in favor of more pressing products. ”They’re quite complicated,“ he said, and Nanoleaf had the best one out there and had “found a pretty good sweet spot” in terms of price and design. Hue could have gone more premium, said Yianni, but that would get expensive. The two companies have been working on the integration for 18 months, choosing a collaboration over integration through Matter, because Matter doesn’t yet carry the dynamic/entertainment functionality Hue wanted. “We wanted it to behave with all of the functionality of a regular Hue product, and there’s a lot that’s not part of the standard yet,” said Yianni. The integration is currently with the Nanoleaf Shapes products, not the Lines, Blocks, or Elements. Starting October 1, 2026, you’ll be able to buy Nanoleaf Hexagon and Triangle starter kits and extensions through starting at $49.99.

articles.title: Anker announces its first over-the-counter hearing aids
articles.summary: Details are slim, but we know they’ll use the Thus chip, which provides excellent vocal quality.
articles.body: In what could be fortuitous timing for hearing aid users, Anker announced its first over-the-counter (OTC) hearing aids at IFA 2026. It was only a couple months ago when LXE Hearing, the parent company for Eargo and Lexie Hearing — two major OTC manufacturers in the US — decided to end US operations and exit the OTC hearing aid market. Now perhaps Anker can fill that void. The receiver-in-canal (RIC) design has a main body that rests behind the ear. It uses Anker’s Thus chip, announced in April and first released in the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro earbuds series. The chip delivers the best voice isolation I’ve ever heard on any audio product and could be an incredible boon for the hearing aids. Anker’s RIC hearing aids use four beam-forming microphones to focus on who the user is speaking to in front of them. They get up to 12 hours of use (up to 36 hours with the case) and gain two hours of use with a five-minute fast charge — Anker claims this is the quickest fast charge among its competitors. There aren’t any additional details about exact models or US availability and pricing, but we should know more by the end of the year.

articles.title: Anker put a display on the case of its new sleepbuds
articles.summary: Anker’s upgraded Sleep Earbuds 4 are 20 percent slimmer for more comfortable side sleeping, while the 4 Pro buds add better monitoring and a display on the case.
articles.body: Anker just announced its new Soundcore Sleep Earbuds 4 and 4 Pro for side-sleepers. They include the same audio masking tech found on last year’s A30 sleepbuds (that can really silent a snoring partner) only now with longer battery life and improved ANC to help silent other noises in the environment. Both sets of buds feature a “20 percent smaller contact area” than the A30 buds, which should reduce pressure and make them more comfortable to wear. They also come with new cases that can be charged on a wireless charging pad, but only the 4 Pro’s case has a display because Anker can’t stop putting screens on things. When streaming music, podcasts, or audiobooks over the buds’ upgraded Bluetooth v6.0 radio, you’ll now get 8 hours of life with ANC on or 11 hours with ANC off, according to Anker. Local playback of audio soundscapes is estimated at 9.5 hours (ANC on) or 14.5 hours (ANC off). The SleepHub case that comes with the 4 Pro buds can control the buds without a phone. That means you can use the integrated OLED display to swipe through preset soundscapes, check your sleep stats, set an alarm, and more. Both the SleepHub case and regular Earbuds 4 case (that still requires a phone) support wireless charging pads for added convenience. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The Earbuds 4 Pro add an in-ear PPG sensor like modern earbuds sold by Sennheiser, Bose, Apple and others to measure real-time stress, fatigue, and recovery levels. Anker will use it to monitor your sleep state, heart rate, and HRV to assess your sleep status and then “facilitate relaxation into sleep” by playing “adaptive soothing audio tracks using Soundcore’s BioSync feature.” That’s something we’ll have to test. The Sleep Earbuds 4 model will launch in October for $229.99 / £199.99 in choice of white and blue, with a pink option coming at a later date. The Sleep Earbuds 4 Pro will arrive a bit later in November in slightly different shades of white and blue, for $349.99 / £299.99. Or, maybe save some money and purchase a much cheaper piercing pillow and just side-sleep with the earbuds you already own.

articles.title: I want to wrap myself in Hue’s new Liane rope lights
articles.summary: The company showcased new architectural lighting that’s designed to be seen.
articles.body: I love smart lighting, but I don’t love many of the form factors it comes in. With a few exceptions, most smart, color-changing lamps and fixtures fit better in my teenage son’s dorm room than my living room. So, I was pleasantly surprised to see Philips Hue’s new line of architecturally focused smart lights, launched at IFA this week and now available to buy at Philips-Hue.com. I was very impressed by the Liane 360-degree Rope Lights, which I saw displayed in a trendy Berlin loft. Its versatility, range of brightness, rich colors, and infinite design possibilities really put the smart into smart lighting. [Image: This collection of 17 weighted 3-meter Liane rope lights crafted into a chandelier will set you back $7,000. Using Hue’s OmniGlow technology, the Liane offers a 360-degree tube of diffuse light that emits in every direction without harsh pinpricks of light. This makes it capable of being a focal point in a room — both decor and illumination. A flexible rope light, the Liane can be hung from a wall or ceiling and shaped into organic forms, using clear clips and mounts, or draped around furniture or architectural features. [Image: You can change them to any color combination you like using the Hue app. This type of light is common in modern interior design, integrating the light source as an architectural feature, but it’s almost always just white light. Hue’s innovation here is bringing smart, color-changing lighting. The catch is that Liane Rope Lights are expensive, starting at $399.99 for 3 meters, with the 5-meter model costing a whopping $549.99. [Image: [Image: Along with the Liane, Hue has added three new lights to its popular Signe line, also designed to be used as interior design features. The Signe pendant, Signe pendulum, and Signe pole feature a slim black housing that can be hung from the ceiling, propped against a wall, or used in other strategic ways to incorporate both design and light. They start at $319.99 beginning in October. Hue also showed off new entries in the popular Festavia indoor/outdoor line, including curtains, nets, and icicle lights. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Photos by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

articles.title: Anker’s new MindBase is an AI-powered brain for your smart home
articles.summary: The company also announced a new Eufy video doorbell with VR features and a window camera.
articles.body: Anker is launching the Eufy MindBase, a local AI hub for its security cameras that runs an on-device, Anker-developed LLM, which the company says can process your footage without it ever leaving your home. It’s also announcing a handful of other smart home security products at the IFA tech show in Berlin this week, including the TrackLight Cam S1, the S4 video doorbell, and a window camera. Pitched as the “central brain for the home,” the MindBase is not just for Eufy security cameras; Anker is positioning it as a whole-home connectivity solution with on-device compute and local storage. Security is the first use case, but the company plans to add an energy agent for your home’s power, a clean agent for your robot vacuums, and more. Anker hasn’t revealed the price or release date yet. Eufy got into trouble a few years back for claiming its cameras were end-to-end encrypted when they weren’t always. It has since overhauled its systems, focusing on local storage and end-to-end encryption. Anker says the MindBase will be a Matter controller, running Matter 1.5, and will support over 40 Matter device categories, including lights, sensors, and HVAC systems. Eufy Security spokesperson Janet Jin told The Verge they plan to integrate Matter-compatible third-party cameras. The MindBase has dual-band Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Thread, and Zigbee and will work with Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video, meaning connected cameras can work with Apple’s smart home system. It can also connect to Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and Home Assistant. It will support 16 wireless cameras and four wired cameras, along with 34 sensors. This includes a new Smart Security Shield sensor that uses 180-degree dual radar to detect movement. Anker says it will work with a digital credential stored on household members’ phones to recognize friends and family and reduce unnecessary alerts. [Image: With up to 48TB of expandable storage and a dedicated AI chip, the MindBase can process events directly for advanced AI features, including natural-language search across recordings and event summaries, without a monthly fee. It also supports smart alerts for facial recognition, people, car, pet, and stranger detection. One of the first products designed to work with MindBase is the upcoming Anker Eufy TrackLight Cam S1, which will be part of an Anker MindBase Security Kit. Anker says this is an active-deterrence camera with an auto-tracking light, 180-degree dual-radar detection, and 4K resolution. Anker says Mindbase will also support a wide range of existing security cameras, such as eufyCam S4. [Image: The Eufy S4 features a panoramic field of view. Anker’s new wired Eufy S4 video doorbell, launching this week, will be compatible with Mindbase. The S4’s other party trick is an “immersive virtual reality (VR)-inspired mobile experience,” according to the company. It shows panoramic footage in the Eufy app allowing you to look around the scene by moving your smartphone. The S4 will cost $299.99 and features a 180-by-180 panoramic field of view, AI-powered tracking and auto-zoom, and 3K-capable recording. It has 64GB of onboard storage, supports Wi-Fi 6, uses a combination of radar and PIR for motion detection. [Image: [Image: A $70 window camera arrives later this year. The E10 is designed for people who can’t install security cameras outside and sticks to the inside of a window to record in full-color night vision. It has on-device person and sound detection. The company also has a new mmWave fall detection sensor. The Eufy Fall Detection Sensor (no price or release date) can be mounted on a wall or ceiling to detect falls and will automatically initiate a voice check after a detected fall or prolonged inactivity. It supports two-way communication and its self-monitoring features don’t require a subscription.

articles.title: Philips Hue adds more affordable options for syncing smart lights with your TV
articles.summary: There are two new ways to sync your lights, both under half the price of the old 8K sync box.
articles.body: Philips Hue is slashing the steep entry price of its entertainment sync offerings. The new stripped-down Sync Box 4K starts at $150, compared to $385 for the 8K model. The brand also launched its first camera-based solution, the Play Screen Sync, for $119.99. Both were on display this week at the IFA tech show in Berlin and are going on sale right away. The sync systems connect to Philips Hue’s color-changing lighting to make your lights move along with the content on your TV, whether that’s games, movies, or cable news. The Sync Box models use HDMI to pull visuals from any device connected to the TV, such as a streaming box or game console, while the camera model works with any content on screen. The camera pairs a fish-eye lens placed at the top of the screen with automatic calibration and color-matching technology. [Image: The Play HDMI sync box 4K costs $149.99 and features a single HDMI input. Signify, which makes Philips Hue, says the HDMI sync boxes are more accurate than the camera-based Screen Sync. But there are advantages to the camera version, too, since the HDMI models can’t sync with content played through apps and services built into your TV. The Sync Box 4K only supports one HDMI input, too, compared to the four on the 8K model. It also uses HDMI 2.0 instead of 2.1 and supports 4K at 60Hz. [Image: Philips Hue has a new camera-based entertainment sync system. Several competitors already have cheaper camera-based sync options; Govee’s start at $90. Philips Hue’s head of technology, George Yianni, says Hue’s solution is different because it’s simple to install. The team built algorithms that auto-detect the TV panel type, ambient room lighting, and white-balance correction — plus automatic detection of the screen corners, he said. “With other devices you have to go through quite some steps to make it work well, and people don’t,” Yianni said. “So they don’t get a great experience out of the box. That’s not the case with ours.” All three Hue Sync solutions now have a new option to work directly with one of the brand’s Play strip lights without requiring a Hue bridge. This lowers the cost of entry further and also makes setup easier. If you decide you want to add more lights, you can add a bridge later. [Image: Philips Hue Play gradient Strip Light Pro comes in 65-, 85- and 100-inch versions. Signify also launched a new line of Hue Play gradient strip lights to go with the sync options, and it will sell starter kits with a bundled strip. The strip lights are now cuttable to fit more TV sizes, and there’s a new Pro version with black housing and Hue’s uniform OmniGlow technology that can fit TVs up to 100 inches. It starts at $179.99 for 65 inches and is available September 15.

articles.title: Belkin’s first trackers come ready to attach to your gear.
articles.summary: The four new trackers work with either Apple’s Find My or Google’s Find Hub tracking networks.
articles.body: After selling accessories for attaching Apple’s AirTags to everything from keys to backpacks, Belkin is introducing its own trackers that work with either Apple’s Find My or Google’s Find Hub tracking networks. In addition to compatibility with Android and iOS, what differentiates these trackers from AirTags and Google’s recently announced Pixel Tag is that you don’t need to buy any additional accessories, cases, or hardware to attach them to items. They come with lanyards or key rings already integrated into their designs. [Image: The $15 Belkin SureFind Spot (left) and $25 SureFind Loop Cable Tag (right). The cheapest and simplest option is the $14.99 Belkin SureFind Spot that comes tethered to a metal key ring, but for $24.99 the SureFind Loop Cable Tag comes with extra functionality in the form of a secure carry loop that doubles as a short USB-C to USB-C charging cable. Both are expected to be available sometime this month. [Image: The $27 Belkin SureFind Card (left) and $40 SureFind Wallet Stand (right). To keep tabs on your wallet without adding a lot of extra bulk the $26.99 SureFind Card is a credit card–sized alternative that comes with an IP68 rating. It can survive a “prolonged submersion in water” according to Belkin, but since Bluetooth doesn’t work under water you’ll have to rely on the tracker’s last known location to find it. Belkin’s most expensive tracker is its $39.99 SureFind Wallet Stand that attaches to mobile devices with magnets, functions as a fold-out stand, and protects your payment cards from wireless snooping by blocking RFID signals. While the SureFind Card is launching this month, you’ll have to wait until October for the Wallet Stand to become available.

articles.title: Belkin introduces its first longer-lasting semi-solid-state power banks
articles.summary: Belkin’s first power banks with semi-solid-state cell technology are slimmer, safer, and longer-lasting.
articles.body: Belkin is joining companies like BMX, Kuxiu, and Zens with the launch of its first power banks featuring semi-solid-state battery technology. The company claims the new accessories have been “engineered to last up to 3x longer than other power banks” with the addition of a “gel-like layer” alongside the liquid electrolyte typically found in lithium-ion batteries. Other advantages of what Belkin is calling its BoostSolid Cell technology include a reduced risk of overheating that could cause swelling or fires and consistent power delivery across a wider temperature range. They’re more expensive than power banks with comparable specs, but a longer functional lifespan should outweigh the premium pricing. [Image: Belkin’s new semi-solid-state wireless power bank maxes out at just 15W of power delivery, and even less when charging two devices. The UltraCharge Pro Slim Magnetic Power Bank 5K Qi2 15W with BoostSolid Cell is the smaller and cheaper option of Belkin’s two new power banks at $69.99. The company claims it’s 40 percent slimmer than other 5,000mAh power banks and is designed to magnetically hang on the back of compatible mobile devices and wirelessly deliver up to 15W of power. A USB-C charging port can also be used to power other devices at up to 22.5W, but charging two devices simultaneously drops the output to just 5W wirelessly and 12W with a USB-C cable. [Image: You can charge up to three devices using Belkin’s 10,000mAh semi-solid-state power bank using two USB-C ports and a single USB-A port. The larger UltraCharge Pro Power Bank 10K 60W with BoostSolid Cell and Display offers twice the capacity with a 10,000mAh battery for an extra $20. The $89.99 power bank is also slimmer than competing options with similar capacities thanks to the increased energy density of its semi-solid-state battery tech. Power output maxes out at up to 60W when charging a single device over USB-C, but that drops when up to three devices are connected and charging using a pair of USB-C ports and a single USB-A port. And because putting screens on batteries is now en vogue, this one has a display showing charge level, power output, and the internal temperature.

articles.title: Here’s the first 4K 120Hz UST projector with optical lens shift
articles.summary: Awol Vision’s LuxVision is a 4K 120Hz UST projector with a world’s first optical lens shift to preserve image detail.
articles.body: Detail-preserving optical lens shift is not something you expect to find on an ultra-short throw projector running Google TV, but that’s exactly what you’ll find inside of Awol Vision’s new LuxVision. It also promises to produce an incredibly bright (6000 ISO Lumens) 4K 120Hz image measuring 120 inches when placed just 7.5 inches from the wall. The vertical lens shift is the star here. Most UST projectors use digital trickery to manipulate the image onto the wall or screen behind it. The LuxVision can raise and lower the output optically to preserve the detail in the 4K image without having to move the projector or resort to keystone correction. That makes this, like all USTs, a possible TV replacement if you’ve got enough cash to offset your hatred for ugly black monoliths. LuxVision is available in a number of colors and trims for that very reason. [Image: Customize your expensive TV replacement. Awol Vision is pitching the LuxVision at sports fans by playing up the fluidity of the 4K 120Hz display, which is still a rarity in projectors. It’s also targeting gamers by baking in Dolby Vision Gaming HDR, ALLM, VRR, and an input lag of around 1ms. You also get 3x HDMI 2.1 ports, 1x DisplayPort, and HDMI Multiview to view up to four sources simultaneously. As you might have guessed, these specs won’t come cheap. It’ll list for $5,999 at launch, sometime “around October.” And that’s before you shell out another $1,000 or so for an ALR screen that can dramatically enhance the viewing experience. Starting September 5th, Awol Vision is offering discounts for anyone willing to preorder the LuxVision ahead of the reviews.

articles.title: These new robot lawnmowers trim your edges
articles.summary: At IFA 2026, Anker and Mammotion took the wraps off their newest robot lawnmowers, both of which come with an edger attachment to clean up the sides of your driveway and garden beds.
articles.body: Anker’s new robot lawnmower might take over for your weedwacker, too. Announced at IFA 2026, the Eufy Robot Lawn Mower S2 Max comes with an extendable trimming arm to clean up the grass around your driveway and flowerbeds. The dual-blade mower offers vSLAM navigation that uses built-in cameras to build a 3D map of your yard, eliminating the need to set up boundary wires or a Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) base station. Anker says the Mower S2 Max can map and mow up to 3.7 acres, while handling yards with up to 80 percent (38-degree) slopes. The robot mower is AWD and will launch in May 2027 for €3,999. There’s no word on US pricing or availability yet. [Image: [Image: [Image: As built-in edgers crop up in robot mower models from Segway, Ecovacs, Roborock, and now Anker, even Mammotion is jumping on the bandwagon with the newly announced Luba 4 AWD, which uses an edge-cutting attachment to trim against walls, fences, and garden borders. The Mammotion Luba 4 AWD roves your yard using four cameras on the front, sides, and rear of the device, along with a 360-degree LiDAR system and network RTK, which taps into the cloud for navigation. Mammotion says the three-sensor system helps to ensure “zero dead zones and zero drift.” Additionally, the Luba 4 AWD comes with independent front-wheel steering, helping the mower change directions without U-turns that might leave tracks on your yard. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The Luba 4 AWD is available in three models, with the 3000F cutting up to 0.75 acres and the 6000F handling up to 1.5 acres. The 12000F is designed to cut up to 3 acres, but it doesn’t support the edge-trimming attachment. The dual-disc system on the 3000F and 6000F models supports a wider 17.3-inch cutting width, while the three cutting discs on the 12000F span 20.9 inches. Mammotion plans to open preorders for the Luba 4 AWD later this year, but it hasn’t shared details on pricing yet.

articles.title: TCL’s new Nxtpaper phone offers both e-reader and OLED
articles.summary: The P80 Ultra is TCL’s first Nxtpaper phone with an OLED display.
articles.body: With the P80 Ultra, TCL’s E Ink-esque Nxtpaper phones are finally going OLED. Just like previous LCD models, the phone can switch to a low power, monochromatic display mode that replicates the look of paper when you want to read or minimize distractions. Only now you can switch back to what the company calls a “flagship-level” OLED experience the rest of the time. TCL first revealed the OLED Nxtpaper technology at MWC in March this year, but without any products that took advantage of it. The P80 Ultra is the first, with a 6.83-inch panel that delivers high-end OLED specs in most respects: a 1.5K resolution, 120Hz refresh rates, 3,200 nits of peak brightness, and coverage of 100 percent of the DCI-P3 color space. In fact, TCL argues that its Nxtpaper innovations actually make this OLED better than some other flagship phones, because it benefits from an anti-glare coating that should be among the best on the market. I’ll be getting the chance to try the P80 Ultra in person at IFA this week, and I’m excited to see whether the OLED panel lives up to that promise. [Image: TCL says its Nxtpaper features shouldn’t disrupt the quality of the OLED panel. Like other Nxtpaper handsets, the P80 Ultra will run just like a regular Android phone 90 percent of the time. Flick the dedicated Nxtpaper Key and it switches to Max Ink Mode though, turning the phone into something more akin to an e-reader: a monochromatic, paperlike display; a custom Android UI with fewer apps and notifications; and dedicated software to use it as an e-reader. Max Ink Mode has another benefit, extending the life of the 5,800mAh battery to a full seven days of active use, or up to 26 days of standby time. The phone’s sculpted rear design is intended to feel fairly premium, but the remaining features fit squarely in the upper midrange market. You get 8GB of RAM and up to 512GB storage, a MediaTek Dimensity 7400 Elite chipset, and 45W wired charging. The 50-megapixel, 1/1.56-inch-type main camera should be fairly capable, though TCL’s image processing lags behind that of bigger name rivals. An 8-megapixel ultrawide doesn’t sound especially impressive, but a 50-megapixel, 3x telephoto lens is a welcome inclusion that adds versatility to the cameras. The P80 Ultra is joined by two cheaper models. The P80 Pro features almost all the same specs, including that OLED panel, but drops to a dual rear camera, omitting the telephoto. The regular P80 is a different beast entirely: It keeps the OLED but lacks the Nxtpaper features, removing TCL’s key selling point, and runs on a smaller 5,000mAh battery. All three phones arrive running Android 16. The Ultra and Pro will receive four years of OS updates and seven of security support, while the base P80 gets one fewer Android version update. The new phones are launching in Europe today, with a Latin American release following in October, and the US “a bit later,” TCL told me during a press briefing. The P80 Ultra starts from €549 (about $635), the P80 Pro from €429 ($500), and the P80 from €349 ($400).
